concept.name: Protective put
concept.definition: A protective put is a position long the underlying asset plus a long put option on it, which sets a floor on the position's value: losses below the put strike are offset by gains in the put. It is the options-market analogue of buying insurance on a holding.
concept.intuition: You keep all the upside of owning the stock but pay a premium so that, no matter how far it falls, you can always sell at the strike price.
concept.mechanics: Hold (or buy) 100 shares and buy one put, typically at or below the current price. Maximum loss is limited to (S_0 - K) + premium per share; upside remains open, reduced by the premium. By put-call parity, long stock + long put equals a long call plus cash (a fiduciary call).
concept.formula: Profit at expiration = max(S_T, K) - S_0 - premium, per share; maximum loss = (S_0 - K) + premium.
concept.failure_modes: Chronic put buying is expensive — downside implied volatility (skew) makes protective puts costly, so persistent hedging can erode returns more than the occasional crash would. Hedging only works to expiration; gaps after expiry are unprotected.
concept.misconceptions: A protective put does not eliminate losses — it caps them at a level that already embeds the premium cost. It is also not 'free insurance' financed by anything; the cost is paid explicitly in premium.
concept.example: Own 100 shares of XYZ at $50 and buy the $48 put for $1. If XYZ collapses to $30, the total loss is capped at ($2 + $1) x 100 = $300 instead of $2,000.
